vignette:
Patient: "Captain M."  
Age: 45  
Occupation: Combat Pilot (retired from active duty, now a civilian flight instructor)  
Trauma: Exposure to a terrorist bombing during a humanitarian airlift mission  
PCL-5: 56  

Captain M. sits at the edge of the chair, back straight, hands folded in her lap. She does not lean back. She does not look around the room. Her eyes are fixed on a spot just above my left shoulder, as if she is scanning the airspace for a threat that might appear.

She begins by telling me she is "fine." That is the first word she says. Then she stops, and for a long moment, the only sound is the hum of the building's ventilation system.

"I was on a C-130," she says finally. "We were bringing medical supplies into a forward operating base. It was supposed to be a milk run. Low altitude, short window, nothing we hadn't done a hundred times."

She describes the day: 14 years ago, but she remembers the smell of the hydraulic fluid, the taste of the coffee from the thermos, the weight of her helmet. She was the pilot in command. On final approach, a truck drove onto the runway. It was not supposed to be there. Then a flash. Then the sound-a sound she describes as "the air tearing."

The bomb was a vehicle-borne IED. The blast wave hit the aircraft just as she was flaring for landing. She fought the controls through the shockwave, fought the yaw and the stall warning, fought to keep the nose up. She landed the plane. No one on board was killed. She was awarded a commendation.

But the truck driver was not a soldier. He was a civilian, a local man, she later learned. He had been coerced, his family threatened. The intelligence report came weeks later. She read it once. She has never said his name aloud.

After the incident, she completed her tour. She did not seek help. She did not talk about it. She was promoted, she flew more missions, she trained younger pilots. She told herself the story was over.

But the story was not over.

Now, in the present, she teaches civilian students how to fly small aircraft. She is good at it-patient, precise. But she has begun to notice things. A car backfiring in the parking lot, and she is on the floor of the hangar, her heart hammering, her hands shaking. A student makes a sudden radio call, and she feels a surge of adrenaline so strong she has to excuse herself to the bathroom. She avoids flying over certain regions of the map, though she cannot explain why. She has stopped watching the news entirely.

She sleeps poorly. She dreams of the flash, the yaw, the stall warning. She wakes with her fists clenched. She has begun drinking wine at night-just one glass, then two-to quiet the noise in her head.

She tells me she does not know why she is here. Her commanding officer suggested it. "I don't have flashbacks," she says. "I don't have nightmares every night." But she is irritable with her students. She is short-tempered with her mother on the phone. She has stopped going to the gym, stopped calling friends. She feels a constant low-grade vigilance, as if she is still in the cockpit, scanning for something that might come out of nowhere.

She closes her eyes for a moment. When she opens them, she says, "I landed the plane. Everyone survived. Why can't I just let it go?"

She waits for an answer. I do not give her one. Not yet. She is not ready for that. She is still scanning the airspace.
